```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 5,
  dpi = 96,
  dev = "jpeg",
  dev.args = list(quality = 90),
  out.width = "100%"
)
has_shazam <- requireNamespace("shazam", quietly = TRUE)
imgt_dir <- path.expand(Sys.getenv("SIRUP_IMGT_DIR"))
has_imgt <- nzchar(imgt_dir) && dir.exists(imgt_dir) && has_shazam
has_trees <- has_imgt
```

A clone is a group of B or T cells that descend from one ancestor cell and
share its receptor rearrangement. In germinal centers, B cell clones gain
somatic hypermutations. A lineage tree of a B cell clone shows how its
sequences relate to each other. Spatial AIRR-seq lets you put each tip of
that tree on the tissue.

SIRUP does not reimplement clone calling or tree building. It runs the
Immcantation tools (scoper, dowser, shazam) on the receptor table inside the
SIRUP object. It then adds the spatial part: clone maps, trees paired with
tissue plots, and distances between tips in and between regions.

This vignette uses MG thymus section 2 and its eGC polygons. SIRUP installs
the Immcantation packages that it needs, such as scoper, dowser, and alakazam.

## Set up

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r setup}
extdata <- system.file("extdata", package = "SIRUP")

thymus <- readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial.rds"))
bcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz")) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = gsub(",", "_", sequence_id)) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL,
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x"
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))

sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = thymus,
  receptors = bcrs,
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE,
  polygons_path = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
)
```

The setup also replaces the comma in each `sequence_id` with `_`. dowser
writes trees in Newick format, where a comma separates tips, so it renames
tips that contain one. With the comma gone, the tip names match the receptor
table, and SIRUP can find each tip on the tissue.

## Call clones inside the object

The setup made a SIRUP object without clones. To call clones, run
`scoper::hierarchicalClones()` through `updateReceptors()`.
`updateReceptors()` gives the receptor table to the function as its first
argument, with your other arguments. It then stores the returned table and
validates the object:

```{r call-clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)

sirup
dplyr::n_distinct(getReceptors(sirup)$clone_id)
```

`hierarchicalClones()` groups sequences with the same V gene, J gene, and
junction length whose junctions differ by less than `threshold`. The SIRUP
paper used `threshold = 0.1` for BCRs. TCRs do not mutate, so call TCR clones
with `scoper::identicalClones()`.

The function writes a `clone_id` column, and `updateReceptors()` records it as
the clone field. If a function writes a different column, record it yourself
with `receptor_fields = list(clone = "my_clone_column")`.

## Germlines

A lineage tree starts at the germline sequence of its clone.
`dowser::createGermlines()` reconstructs one germline per clone from the IMGT
reference sequences. The SIRUP paper made the germlines and removed likely
PCR chimeras in the object.

SIRUP does not include the IMGT references. Download them (for example with
the Immcantation script `fetch_imgtdb.sh`) and set `SIRUP_IMGT_DIR` to the
folder that holds the human V, D, and J FASTA files, such as
`~/share/germlines/imgt/human/vdj`. The germline and tree chunks below run only
when that folder exists.

```{r germlines, eval = has_imgt, message = FALSE}
references <- dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir)

sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  references = references,
  id = "sequence_id",
  nproc = 1
)

sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, function(receptors) {
  chimera <- shazam::slideWindowDb(
    receptors,
    sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
    germlineColumn = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
    mutThresh = 6,
    windowSize = 10
  )
  receptors[!chimera, ]
})
```

## Somatic hypermutation

`shazam::observedMutations()` counts the mutations of each sequence against a
germline. With clonal germlines, use `germline_alignment_d_mask`. Here we use
`germline_alignment`, the germline of each sequence that IgBLAST wrote, so the
chunk runs without the IMGT references. The result goes in `mu_freq`, the
fraction of mutated positions:

```{r shm, eval = has_shazam}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  shazam::observedMutations,
  sequenceColumn = "sequence_alignment",
  germlineColumn = "germline_alignment",
  frequency = TRUE,
  combine = TRUE
)
summary(getReceptors(sirup)$mu_freq)
```

`plotReceptors()` can color spots by a numeric receptor column in place of
groups. Give the column to `value`. When a spot has several receptors,
`value_combine` sets how SIRUP combines them (the mean, by default):

```{r shm-map, eval = has_shazam}
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "locus",
  value = "mu_freq",
  value_colors = c("white", "darkred"),
  receptor_size = 1.3,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  title = "Mean SHM frequency per spot"
)
```

## Choose clones

Trees are most useful for expanded clones. Here we choose clones in the eGCs
of this section that have between 10 and 60 sequences:

```{r choose-clones}
clone_sizes <- getReceptors(sirup) %>%
  group_by(clone_id) %>%
  summarise(
    n_sequences = n(),
    n_in_gc = sum(!is.na(polygon_id)),
    n_gcs = n_distinct(na.omit(polygon_id)),
    gcs = paste(sort(unique(na.omit(polygon_id))), collapse = ", ")
  ) %>%
  filter(n_sequences >= 10, n_sequences <= 60, n_in_gc > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_in_gc))

head(clone_sizes)
tree_clones <- head(clone_sizes$clone_id, 3)
```

Show their spots on the tissue:

```{r clone-map}
plotReceptors(
  sirup,
  group = "clone_id",
  group_val = tree_clones,
  receptor_size = 1.6,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  zoom = TRUE,
  title = "Selected clones"
)
```

## Build trees

Two functions run dowser on the object:

* `formatSpatialClones()` runs `dowser::formatClones()` and stores the result as
  an analysis.
* `getSpatialTrees()` runs `dowser::getTrees()` on a stored formatted-clone
  analysis and stores the trees as another analysis.

Both take the dowser arguments. Tree building takes time for large clones, so
first make a smaller object with only the clones you want. `updateReceptors()`
with `dplyr::filter()` does this:

```{r build-trees, eval = has_trees}
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id %in% tree_clones)

tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  analysis_name = "formatted_clones",
  id = "sequence_id",
  germ = "germline_alignment_d_mask",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "polygon_id")
)

tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(
  tree_sirup,
  f_clones_analysis = "formatted_clones",
  analysis_name = "trees",
  build = "pratchet"
)

trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees")
trees
```

`traits` keeps the columns that the tree plots need. Keep the spatial ID, so
SIRUP can put each tip on the tissue, and any column that you want to color
by.

`build = "pratchet"` builds maximum parsimony trees, which is fast. For the
paper we used maximum likelihood (`build = "pml"`). For B cell specific
models, use IgPhyML (`build = "igphyml"` with the `igphyml` path).

Store the trees in the main object:

```{r store-trees, eval = has_trees}
sirup <- setAnalysis(sirup, "trees", trees)
```

## Pair each tree with the tissue

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` makes two plots for each clone: the lineage tree
and a tissue map. Each tip gets one color in both plots, so you can find a
tip of the tree on the tissue:

```{r tree-pairs, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black"
)
names(pairs)

cowplot::plot_grid(
  pairs[[1]]$tree,
  pairs[[1]]$spatial_clone,
  rel_widths = c(1.2, 1)
)
```

The result is a list with one element per clone. Each element holds a `tree`
plot and a `spatial_clone` plot. Tips with a spot in this section are
circles. Tips without one, such as bulk sequences, are squares and appear in
the tree only. Sequences in the same spot share a point on the map.

### Color tips by group

When a clone has many tips, one color per tip is hard to read.
`clusterTreesTips()` cuts each tree into `k` connected groups of related tips.
Here `k = 4` for every tree:

```{r tree-clusters, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
clustered <- clusterTreesTips(
  trees,
  k = 4,
  id = "sequence_id",
  cluster = "tree_cluster"
)

cluster_pairs <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  clustered,
  object = sirup,
  clone_val = tree_clones,
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  zoom = TRUE,
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE
)

cowplot::plot_grid(
  cluster_pairs[[1]]$tree,
  cluster_pairs[[1]]$spatial_clone,
  rel_widths = c(1.2, 1)
)
```

With `k = "auto"`, the function chooses `k` for each tree from `k_range`. It
stops when one more cut reduces the mean within-group patristic distance by
less than `improvement_threshold` (10% by default). A tree with little
structure can get `k = 1`, which gives all its tips one color.

`color_by` accepts any column of the dowser clone data. For example,
`color_by = "polygon_id"` colors each tip by its eGC, because we kept
`polygon_id` in `traits`.

### Save every pair

`spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF()` writes one page per clone:

```{r pdf, eval = FALSE}
spatialCloneTreePairsToPDF(cluster_pairs, "tree_pairs.pdf", width = 12, height = 6)
```

## Tree distance and physical distance

Do sequences in the same eGC have shorter tree distances than sequences in
different eGCs? The patristic distance between two tips is the sum of the
branch lengths between them. `tipPatristicMatrix()` gives these distances for
a set of tips. Here we take the selected clone in the most eGCs, and compare
its tip pairs in the same eGC with its pairs in different eGCs:

```{r patristic, eval = has_trees}
multi_gc_clone <- clone_sizes %>%
  filter(clone_id %in% tree_clones) %>%
  slice_max(n_gcs, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  pull(clone_id)
multi_gc_clone

index <- which(trees$clone_id == multi_gc_clone)
clone_data <- trees$data[[index]]@data
tree <- trees$trees[[index]]

gc_tips <- clone_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(polygon_id), sequence_id %in% tree$tip.label) %>%
  select(sequence_id, polygon_id)

distances <- tipPatristicMatrix(tree, gc_tips$sequence_id)

pairs_table <- as.data.frame(as.table(distances)) %>%
  rename(tip_a = Var1, tip_b = Var2, distance = Freq) %>%
  filter(as.character(tip_a) < as.character(tip_b)) %>%
  mutate(
    gc_a = gc_tips$polygon_id[match(tip_a, gc_tips$sequence_id)],
    gc_b = gc_tips$polygon_id[match(tip_b, gc_tips$sequence_id)],
    pair = if_else(gc_a == gc_b, "same eGC", "different eGCs")
  )

pairs_table %>%
  group_by(pair) %>%
  summarise(n_pairs = n(), median_distance = median(distance))
```

In this clone, tips in the same eGC are closer in the tree than tips in
different eGCs. One clone is not enough for a conclusion, because tip pairs
share branches. In the SIRUP paper we ran this comparison over all GC clones,
with a mixed model and a random effect for each clone.

With `collapse = TRUE` (the default), `formatClones()` merges identical
sequences into one tip, so not every sequence keeps its own tip.
